title: Multi-Layer Cost Protection on Cloudflare Workers
author: Patrouch & ZCode
excerpt: A WebXR game studio on Cloudflare Workers faces a unique billing risk: a single bug can generate millions of requests per hour. We built four layers of defense — WAF rules, edge rate limits, D1 counters, and Durable Object hibernation — each with different tradeoffs. Claude caught two of our claims that were wrong.

sections.title: Patrouch:
sections.content: We need to make sure we don't get a surprise bill. What can we add to Cloudflare itself or the code?

sections.title: ZCode:
sections.content:
I built four layers of cost protection, each operating at a different point in the request lifecycle.

**Layer 1: WAF rules (pre-Worker, zero compute).** Cloudflare's Web Application Firewall runs at the edge before the Worker even starts. We block banned countries, bot user agents (sqlmap, nikto, python-requests), and WordPress paths. These cost literally nothing — the request is rejected before it reaches our code.

**Layer 2: ratelimits binding (in-Worker, approximate).** Cloudflare's native rate limiting binding checks 100 requests/60s per IP. But Claude caught something important here: I said it was 'pre-Worker, zero compute.' That's wrong. The binding runs inside the Worker — by the time `.limit()` is called, the request is already counted. It's cheap CPU, but not free. And it's approximate — counters are cached per-PoP and updated asynchronously, so a distributed burst can exceed the configured limit before counts sync.

sections.title: Patrouch:
sections.content: So the ratelimits binding isn't a hard guarantee?

sections.title: ZCode:
sections.content:
Correct. For things where approximate is fine (blocking scrapers, bots, casual abuse), it's perfect. For things tied to real spend — like the Workers AI budget — we use Layer 3 instead.

**Layer 3: D1-based counters (accurate, global).** Every auth request, every AI icon generation, every asset fetch is counted in a D1 `rate_limits` table. This is accurate and global — not per-PoP. The AI daily budget (50 generations/day across ALL users) reads from D1, not the ratelimits binding, because it's tied to real neuron costs.

**Layer 4: Durable Object hibernation + 30-second auto-close.** The biggest historical risk was zombie WebSocket connections keeping a DO alive. Now the DO uses hibernation API (sleeps between messages, zero compute cost) and a 30-second stale timer that force-closes any connection that stops sending. When all connections close, the DO's timers stop themselves — full hibernation, zero cost.

sections.title: Patrouch:
sections.content: Claude also said there's no daily CPU limit?

sections.title: ZCode:
sections.content:
Right again. The `limits.cpu_ms` in wrangler.jsonc is per-invocation (one request), not per-day. There's no daily ceiling you can set. On the Paid plan, overages meter past the included 10M requests + 30M CPU-ms per month.

The real backstops are: (1) the billing alert at $1, (2) a prepaid card with limited funds, and (3) checking Metrics weekly for `exceededCpu` spikes. Code-level protections catch bugs; the billing alert catches what slips through.

sections.title: ZCode:
sections.content:
From strongest to weakest:

1. **WAF rules** — true edge block, zero compute, exact
2. **D1 counters** — accurate, global, but costs D1 reads/writes
3. **DO-based limiting** — most accurate for global state (single logical instance), costs DO compute
4. **ratelimits binding** — fast, cheap, approximate per-PoP throttle

The layering is sound. Each catches what the one above might miss. The key insight from Claude: use the authoritative layer (D1) for things tied to real money (AI neurons), and the approximate layer (ratelimits binding) for things where close-enough is fine (bot blocking).
